title: One mile across the boundary
hook: Should crossing 100,000 miles create a large step in a car's value?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish smooth wear from a discontinuity at an odometer's round-number boundary.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish smooth wear from a discontinuity at an odometer's round-number boundary.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy car’s price moves from €10,000 to €9,800 at a round mileage boundary. What is the price change? Toy inputs A=[10000, 9800, -1]; B=[10000, 9999, -1].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[-200, -1, -199], [-1, -1, 0]]. Labels: Observed change €, Smooth change €, Extra jump €.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The boundary case has a discrete jump compared with the smooth one-mile depreciation rule. The difference isolates a discontinuity in this toy price schedule; it does not mean physical wear jumps at the displayed number.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Before price €=10000, After price €=9999, Smooth change €=-1. What is Observed change €? Answer: -1.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Before price €=10000, After price €=9999, Smooth change €=-1. What is Observed change €?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives -1. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Used-car prices drop discretely each time the odometer crosses a 10,000-mile mark (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, 2012).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish smooth wear from a discontinuity at an odometer's round-number boundary.
